content_voiceover: This is the classic red cell membrane cytoskeleton diagram, and it is high yield because the two types of protein interactions map directly onto two different diseases. Vertical interactions connect the lipid bilayer to the underlying spectrin cytoskeleton, via band 3, ankyrin, and protein 4.2 on one axis, and glycophorin C with protein 4.1R on the other. When vertical interactions fail, the membrane destabilizes, buds off, and you get spherocytosis. Horizontal interactions are the side to side connections between spectrin dimers, alpha and beta spectrin self associating into tetramers, and connecting through protein 4.1R, actin, and adducin to glycophorin C. When horizontal interactions fail, the cell cannot maintain its shape under shear stress, giving you elliptocytosis. Band 3 anchors the vertical connection to ankyrin and also carries CD47 and Rh proteins, while GPA and GPC are surface glycophorins. The core teaching point for boards, vertical defect equals spherocytosis, horizontal defect equals elliptocytosis.
keypoints: Band 3 anchors bilayer to ankyrin; carries Rh, CD47
α/β spectrin tetramers form the horizontal skeletal lattice
keypoint_voiceover: Remember this one rule, vertical protein interactions, band 3, ankyrin, protein 4.2, connecting the membrane to the spectrin skeleton, when defective cause spherocytosis. Horizontal interactions, the spectrin-spectrin self association and the 4.1R-actin-adducin complex, when defective cause elliptocytosis. That vertical versus horizontal distinction is the single most testable fact from this diagram.
